experiments.learned: Calibrate on known text cut to your own band height. A score tuned on tall known-text segments overstates what a short band can show, and makes a null look stronger than it is. The control kit now does this for any band height (--band-mm). Taller bands would make every check more sensitive: 2–3 cm shows 4–5 lines instead of two.

experiments.title: PHerc0813 re-check with Reader v2 + d9v4C: the high scorers are rows of crack blobs, not letters
experiments.question: All 50 outer PHerc0813 windings, re-scored with the fixed row score: what is at the top, and does it look like writing next to known text at the same scale?
experiments.technique: Final scoring pass of the overnight maps (Reader v2 + d9v4C, depths 0 and +1) with the finished row score; the six windings over the provisional line viewed at full resolution in reading orientation, reading side next to the CT, beside the PHerc0841 known text rendered and inked the same way.
experiments.result: Eight winding-depths on six windings passed the provisional row rule: w094 (row 2.63, blind 0.55), w102 (2.44 / 0.29), w076 (2.31 / 0.56), w093, w109 and w070 (w070–w072 repeat the same pattern turn after turn). At full resolution none of them looks like writing: known text shows crisp, elongated, curved strokes; these show soft round blobs, and the CT under every window has cracks or delamination running along the winding (image).

images.caption: Top: known text (PHerc0841, Reader v2 + d9v4C, depth +1), reading and blind side, about 2 × 1.2 cm. Below: the three highest PHerc0813 windows at the same scale, reading side and the CT under it. Text gives crisp, elongated strokes; the PHerc0813 marks are round blobs over crack fields.

experiments.learned: On a crack-rich scroll the row score alone cannot tell rows of letters from rows of crack blobs. What told them apart by eye was the shape of the marks, so stroke-score 0.2 gets a shape score.

experiments.title: A stroke-shape score: are the marks long thin strokes or round blobs?
experiments.question: Letters are made of strokes; crack edges and damage give blobs. Can a number capture what the eye used to reject the PHerc0813 candidates?
experiments.technique: For every above-background mark: area, length and width from its second moments, elongation, peak height and edge contrast, measured on known text (PHerc0139, PHerc0841), on their blind sides, on the PHerc0813 candidates and on null windings of both scrolls. The score is the share of the marks' area in marks at least 1 mm long and twice as long as wide, measured in the window where the row score found rows.
experiments.result: Calibrated. The share of the marks' area in long thin marks separates known text (median 0.42–0.63 per 1 cm strip) from crack rows on PHerc0813 (0.15–0.21). The 0.2 rule flags rows of strokes (row and shape thresholds per model set) or a strong reading-blind contrast (added after the PHerc. 0343 check). On 771 null winding-depths it flags four, all checked by eye. A "streak" column flags the one remaining false-alarm type, crack edges drawn as long streaks along the winding. Released as stroke-score 0.2.0 (git tag stroke-score-v0.2.0).

images.caption: The false alarm the 0.2 rule still flags, PHerc0813 w079 (Reader v2 + d9v4C, depth 0): long marks (orange), but all of them lie flat along a crack. The streak column reports this; a look at the CT settles it.

experiments.learned: Letters are strokes; cracks are blobs and streaks. Shape is what told them apart by eye, and now it is a number.

experiments.short: Tall bands on PHerc0813: the 2.3 cm band
experiments.title: Brute force, option 1: tile the scroll with taller bands, starting with 2.3 cm on PHerc0813
experiments.question: We have searched about 1 cm of PHerc0813's 15.9 cm. Does our fit recipe hold on a band 2.5 times taller, so that we can tile the whole scroll, and do taller windings make text easier to see?
experiments.technique: The exp-30k spiral-fit recipe on z 10,500–13,000 (2,500 slices, 2.3 cm), which contains our best 1 cm band (z 12,000–13,000, satisfied tracks 0.557 / 0.182); then snap, flatten, render, ink with Reader v2 + d9v4C and score with stroke-score 0.2. Gate after the snap: fit metrics and QA before anything is inked. On the home GPUs.
experiments.result: The 2.3 cm fit held: satisfied track points 0.526 and tracks 0.160 (the 1 cm band: 0.557 and 0.182), 88 % of mesh points on a predicted sheet after the snap. All 76 windings (w040–w115) were inked with Reader v2 + d9v4C at depths 0 and +1 (304 runs) and scored with stroke-score 0.2: three flags (w083, w043, w066), none writing. w083 is a diffuse cloud where the fit put three windings (w082–w084) on one sheet; w043 and w066 are bright clusters at the strip's edge, next to cracks that run through the neighbouring turns. The next band, z 8,000–10,500, is rendered and being inked.
experiments.learned: The recipe tiles: a 2.3 cm band fits about as well as a 1 cm one. In places the fit stacks two or three windings on one sheet (neighbours under 0.1 mm apart with identical CT), which leaves other sheets unsearched; we will measure that before trusting a band's coverage.

experiments.short: Ink first: 80 % of the mesh pipeline, no mesh
experiments.title: Brute force, option 3: find ink first, build geometry only where it is
experiments.question: Our search only covers surface where we have good meshes, and meshes are the slow, fragile part. Can the ink models find text from the published surface predictions alone, with no mesh, so that compute can sweep a whole scroll?
experiments.technique: On a 1.2 × 1.2 cm block of PHerc0139 around the densest known text of w047: points on the published recto-surface prediction about every 0.9 mm; at each point the normal from the local shape of the prediction; a 66-layer patch cut along that normal like a tiny render; all patches tiled into one mosaic and inked with the same models and scripts as our renders; the results mapped back to 3D and onto w047, where the text is known.
experiments.result: Tested on two known-text segments with models that never trained on them (we first used d9v4C on PHerc0139 w047, which it was trained on; those runs are discarded, see notes/inkfirst-2026-10-11.md). On PHerc0841, a scroll none of the 9 µm models saw, against human ink labels: AUC 0.76 and correlation 0.45 at 49 % coverage (z +5 against 72 shifted labels), against 0.81 and 0.57 for our full mesh pipeline on the same pixels, so about 80 % of its signal with no geometry work. On PHerc0139 w047 (Reader v2): correlation 0.33 at 50 % coverage, 0.28 at 74 % with blending (z +6). As a coarse ink-density map (0.5 mm cells) 0.59 on PHerc0841. Within one scroll it agrees with the mesh pipeline on the same windings (per winding r 0.2–0.6 on PHerc0813 and PHerc0191). Not shown yet: telling text regions from text-free ones; a text block has three to ten times more high-contrast patches than two text-free blocks, but those two differ from each other by four times. Packaged as tools/ink-first 0.1.

images.caption: PHerc0841, a scroll the models never trained on, 1.2 × 1.2 cm: the human ink labels, our mesh pipeline (Reader v2), and ink first with no mesh (Reader v2; blue: no patch landed). The ink-first patches are brighter near the letters, which is what the AUC of 0.76 measures, but the picture is a patchwork, not readable text.

Ink first in a CT slice across PHerc0841 through a line of writing (Reader v2, no mesh): the patches lie along the sheets and are painted with the ink prediction (dim: below the block's median). Zoom: the labelled sheet coloured by ink first, next to the same sheet coloured by the human ink labels; ink first is brighter on the labelled ink (0.45 against 0.33 at this height). Bottom: a PHerc0813 block with no text found, same colour scale (its patches are 0.9 mm apart instead of 0.6 mm). Two text-free scrolls differ from each other about as much, so this does not show yet that ink first separates text from no text.

experiments.learned: Ink can be found in 9 µm scans without a fitted mesh, at most of the mesh pipeline's strength, on an unseen scroll. Next: coverage (snapping each patch onto the surface), and a test inside one scroll of whether it points at text regions. Prior art: the organisers segment ink directly in 3D on PHerc. Paris 4 at 2.4 µm, where ink is visible; we have not found this approach at 9 µm.

experiments.title: Would stroke-score 0.2 have found the only First Letters win? At first not; now with every model set
experiments.question: Erwin Nieuwlaar's PHerc. 0343 segment is the one First Letters win so far. Does our final 0.2 rule flag it?
experiments.technique: stroke-score 0.2 on his 66-layer render (8.64 µm) at depth +1 with four model sets: his three and four models, Reader v2 + d9v4C, and all six. Also in strips as tall as our 1 cm search bands.
experiments.result: With the rows-of-strokes rule alone it did not: his letters are faint and sparse and form weak rows (row score 0.4–1.4), and his mesh is too ragged (62 % of the frame has data) to score in 1 cm strips. What it does show strongly is more stroke area on the reading side than on the blind side of the same sheet: +0.030 to +0.036, while our 771 null winding-depths never pass +0.016 with three or four models and +0.024 with Reader v2 + d9v4C. So the 0.2 rule now has two lines, rows of strokes or reading-blind contrast, with thresholds per model set; the PHerc. 0343 segment is flagged with every model set, and the false alarms on our nulls stay the same few windings we had already checked by eye (image).

images.caption: What stroke-score sees on the PHerc. 0343 First Letters segment (Nieuwlaar; four models, depth +1, reading orientation): ink marks over the CT, long thin (stroke-shaped) marks in orange, round marks in blue; reading side, the blind side of the same sheet, and the across-row profile (two peaks: two lines of letters).
The same view of a false alarm, PHerc0813 w094 (Reader v2 + d9v4C): two rows, so a high row score (2.6), but the marks are round blobs along crack edges, not strokes.

experiments.learned: Test a search tool on the one known win before trusting it. Text at the limit of detection does not look like the clear text we calibrated on; the two lines cover both kinds.

experiments.title: Where we have looked: every searched winding on a CT slice of each scroll
experiments.question: How much of PHerc0191 and PHerc0813 has the search covered so far, and where were the flags?
experiments.technique: A CT slice across the scroll (from above) and one along its axis through the centre (from the side), with every fitted winding drawn where its mesh crosses the slice: grey for fitted only, blue for rendered, inked and scored, orange for flagged by stroke-score 0.2 and checked by eye. box/bin/viz_looked.py.
experiments.result: PHerc0813: 58 windings searched in the 1 cm band at 112–122 mm, one flag (w079, crack-edge streaks); the 2.3 cm band at 98–122 mm (76 windings) is being scored, and 75–98 mm is being fitted. PHerc0191: 129 windings in two 1 cm bands (84–94 and 105–114 mm), two flags (w061, fibre streaks; w087, a zone that recurs on neighbouring windings). The search reaches a good share of the outer windings but only a band or two of each scroll's height.

images.caption: PHerc0813 from above (CT slice at 117 mm) and from the side (through the centre). Blue: windings rendered, inked and scored; orange: flagged by stroke-score 0.2 and checked by eye (w079, crack-edge streaks); light blue: the 2.3 cm band being scored; hatched: being fitted; grey: fitted, not searched.
PHerc0191, the same view (CT slice at 110 mm): two searched 1 cm bands; orange: w061 (fibre streaks) and w087 (a recurring zone), both checked by eye.

experiments.learned: Seen from the side, each searched band is a thin slice of the scroll. Taller bands are how to cover more of it.

experiments.title: Does stroke-score 0.2 hold on text it never saw, and does it beat plain ink measures?
experiments.question: The 0.2 thresholds were set on three known-text segments, and the contrast line was added after the PHerc. 0343 check. Do they hold on new text, and is the rule better than simply measuring how much ink the models see?
experiments.technique: Thresholds frozen first: tag stroke-score-v0.2.0. Held-out text: PHerc0841 w00, the sheet next to our 0841 control (about 0.4 mm away, so different text), on a scroll none of the 9 µm models trained on; rendered from the public CT, inked with both model sets, cut into 1 cm strips like our search bands. Baselines and ranking: known-text strips and the null windings scored with the same code; the 0.2 rule against mean ink probability, ink area and their reading-blind differences, at the same number of false alarms on the nulls, and where known text lands when it is mixed into the null ranking. On the home GPUs.
experiments.result: Thresholds frozen at stroke-score-v0.2.0, then scored on PHerc. 0841 w00, the neighbouring sheet of the 0841 control: new text that no 9 µm model trained on. With Reader v2 + d9v4C the 0.2 rule flags 14 of its 15 one-centimetre strips; with the three models (ink_9um ×2 + dense_native), 6 of 15. On the null windings it flags 8 of 294 winding-depths (Reader v2 + d9v4C) and 0 of 194 (three models); every flag was checked by eye: crack streaks and bright zones that recur on the neighbouring turns. Known-text strips against nulls: AUC 0.895 and 0.968. Plain ink amounts score as high (up to 0.99) but also tell the two text-free scrolls apart (AUC 0.95), so across scrolls they measure the scan, not the text. Mixed into the null ranking, the 0.2 margin puts 3.8 of 4.7 and 7.5 of 8.5 known strips in the top 20. On the way we found a bug: isolated invalid pixels zeroed the row score of renders with many one-pixel specks.
experiments.learned: The rule holds on new text with Reader v2 + d9v4C and is weaker with the three-model set on faint text. Released as stroke-score 0.2.1: same thresholds, the speck fix, and these numbers in the README. 0.2.2 fixes 0.2.1's packaging: an old build copy in the repository could be installed instead of the fixed code.

experiments.short: Ink first over all of PHerc0175A (AWS)
experiments.title: Brute force, option 3 at scale: ink first over a whole 8.64 µm scroll
experiments.question: Can ink first, which needs no mesh, sweep a whole scroll in an evening and point at text?
experiments.technique: PHerc0175A, the clearest of the 8.64 µm eligible scans, tiled into 199 blocks of 1280³ voxels. In each block, patches cut along the sheets of the published surface prediction (one point per 0.8 mm cube), inked with Reader v2 in both layer orders, summarised per block and mapped over the scroll. Four g5.4xlarge on AWS, about four hours, $25.50 on demand.
experiments.result: 129,125 patches over the whole scroll, no failures, and nothing writing-like. Hot patches are about as common on the reading side as on the other (1.42 % and 1.31 %), and the hottest are saturated blobs on cracks, holes and crushed fibres. The positive control on PHerc. 343 afterwards (next entry) showed that this sampling puts too few patches on any one sheet for a small written area to stand out, so the quiet map rules out large, strongly inked areas, not a few lines of text.

images.caption: PHerc0175A from above and from the side, every ink-first patch coloured by how much of its centre Reader v2 inks on the reading side; grey = looks like damage. The hot spots are scattered through the scroll and sit on damage; no region stands out.

experiments.learned: A whole-scroll sweep is cheap (an evening, about $25), but at one point per 0.8 mm cube it is a coarse net. Next: a sampler that takes a point on every sheet, tested first on PHerc. 343.

experiments.short: Ink first on known 8.64 µm letters (PHerc. 343)
experiments.title: Does ink first see real 8.64 µm letters? A positive control on PHerc. 343
experiments.question: Before trusting a quiet PHerc0175A: does ink first light up on letters we know are there, in the same kind of scan?
experiments.technique: One block of PHerc. 343 holding 10 of Erwin Nieuwlaar's 18 First Letters (his letter boxes placed in 3D through his published mesh), cut and inked exactly like the PHerc0175A sweep (Reader v2 and d9v4C); every patch mapped back onto his segment.
experiments.result: Half yes. Where patches land on his letters they light up on the reading side only (15 % of letter patches hot with Reader v2 and 23 % with d9v4C, against 1 % on other sheets), and they match the mesh pipeline's map of the same spots (r 0.72). But only 13 of the block's 766 patches land on letters: one point per 0.8 mm cube is spread over many sheets. A sampler that takes a point on every sheet piece in each cube found 4,441 patches in the same block; that run is being inked.

images.caption: Nieuwlaar's PHerc. 343 segment in reading orientation. Grey: our Reader v2 map from the mesh pipeline, with his letters inside the boxes. Squares: ink-first patch centres (1.1 mm), coloured by how much they ink, filled when hot. Top: reading side; bottom: the other side. Most letters get no patch at all.

experiments.learned: Ink first can see 8.64 µm ink, but it needs denser sampling to find it.

experiments.short: Is the ink in the raw CT?
experiments.title: Is there an ink signal in the raw CT itself, without a model?
experiments.question: The CT shows the papyrus weave, cracks and holes in fine detail but never the ink. Is the ink in the data at all at 8.64 µm, and can we see it without a model?
experiments.technique: On Nieuwlaar's PHerc. 343 segment: the CT brightness along the normal inside the letter strokes against the papyrus between them; the same split by where the surface sits inside a voxel; plain-CT images made to bring out a brighter written face.
experiments.result: The ink is in the CT: inside the strokes the CT is about 8 units brighter (about 6 % of the scan's range) through the written sheet, peaking two voxels in. Where the surface sits inside a voxel matters a little (about 15 % weaker contrast in the worst quarter), because the scan's blur spreads the ink over two or three voxels. But no plain-CT image shows the letters: the weave, cracks and holes are far stronger. The models' map shows them plainly.

images.caption: PHerc. 343, Nieuwlaar's letters (boxes) in reading orientation. Top three panels: CT only (the rendered layer; the written face, smoothed; the written face minus the gap in front). Bottom: the five-model ink map. The letters show only in the bottom panel. 1 cm bars.

experiments.learned: At 8–9 µm only trained models pull the ink out of the texture, so better models for this kind of scan are the main lever.

experiments.title: Real letters light up in every model; false alarms in some
experiments.question: Our false alarms often show in one or two models only. Does counting how many of six independently trained models see a spot one-sided separate letters from damage?
experiments.technique: Six models (Nieuwlaar's four, Reader v2 and d9v4C) on PHerc. 343 at the letters' depth, and our six-model deep look at PHerc0813 w079 (a spot Ted picked in the viewer): per tile, how many models see the reading side brighter than the blind side by more than a fifth of their own spread.
experiments.result: At least five of the six agree on 78 % of 343's 18 letters, on 10 % of 39 tiles of its bare papyrus, and on 25 % of the w079 spot's 8 tiles; there, only the two models that flagged it saw a one-sided signal, and no model shows strokes. The same test on clean papyrus of PHerc0813 and PHerc0191 is running.
experiments.learned: Agreement is the first rule we have that separates real letters from the crack-and-hole false alarms; it goes into triage if it holds on 9.36 µm papyrus.

findings.title: The ink detector is not the problem
findings.text: Calibrated on known text: three legible Greek lines, the PHerc. 343 control passes with the ensemble, and at 9.36 µm our render and ink steps reproduce the published AUCs on PHerc0139 and PHerc0841 (run 7). The early PHerc0191 nulls were geometry; since the snap + flatten the windings have clean papyrus weave. What limits our nulls now is the triage rule that decides where we look, not the detector (see below).

findings.title: Positive control passes only with the ensemble
findings.text: On the PHerc. 343 winning segment our four-model ensemble shows the letter rows; ink_9um seed 42 alone at whole-segment scale does not. Searches on 0191 need the ensemble (Hecate is the strongest single model).

findings.title: Minimal-route spiral fits sit on the sheet ~46–49% of the time
findings.text: Satisfaction = within 6 voxels and 0.45 winding of the track's sheet. Weights don't help; 3× steps gives +3 points.

findings.title: The fitted spiral never reaches the outer third
findings.text: Per-sector audit: outermost winding 3–8 mm short of the boundary in the fat sectors; initial spacing fixes the radial extent; stretching hurts the inner tracks.

findings.title: Crushed scroll = same winding count, 2.5× spacing variation by sector
findings.text: 0.13 mm on the flattened sides (ray audit under-counts there) to 0.26 mm at the ends. Needs anisotropic deformation or local spacing supervision.

findings.title: Patch growing needs its normal grids
findings.text: Without normal_grid_path the tracer produces data-independent discs. With them it partly follows sheets.

findings.title: #1 libvolcomp not installed by the VC3D build (merged upstream, villa #2008)
findings.text: One-line CMake install fix; merged on 2026-10-12.

findings.title: #2–#5 image tags, lockfile rewrite, remote-fetch aborts
findings.text: :stable tag missing; uv.lock rewritten by sync; infer and renderer abort on a single transient remote chunk fetch. Since then upstream: vc_render_tifxyz takes a remote URL as --volume (villa #1863), and a retry for inference is open as villa #1919 (not ours).

findings.title: #6 Shipped track-crossing cache rejected after download (in review, villa #2020)
findings.text: Signature uses nanosecond mtime; any download zeroes sub-second mtime. 2.4 GB downloaded for nothing; every run rebuilds. After review the fix covers all three checks, and it still catches a local edit within the same second (my first version did not; a test caught it).

findings.title: #7 Outer-shell loss silently zero for sparse shells (villa #2021, awaiting review)
findings.text: Confidence normalized by an edge spike → 0.22 < 0.25 → no valid samples, no warning. Reproduced outside the fitter.

findings.title: #8 Fiber inference needs lasagna on PYTHONPATH (merged upstream, villa #2019)
findings.text: geometry.py imports lasagna.omezarr_pyramid unguarded; the models extra does not ship it.

findings.title: The PHerc. 343 First Letters win (2026-10-08) used our pipeline plus three steps we lacked
findings.text: Spiral fit with the surface-prediction distance field, no shell, 30k steps; post-hoc snap of every vertex onto the nearest predicted sheet (±15 vox); 66-layer render swept over 31 depths through a four-model ink ensemble. All open source; adopted (see notes/prior-art-digest.md).

findings.title: PHerc0191: no letters where we looked
findings.text: Band z 9,000–10,000: all 99 flattened windings at depths 0 and +1 (7 four-model, 92 three-model). The community's 10 windings. The seven best clear-band windings at depths −2..+3 with four models. Phase A4 on the other 93: 60 rows over the v0.1 flag line, 25 checked by eye, none writing. But we looked closely only where the v0.1 rule flagged, and that rule misses text on an unseen scroll, so these nulls are weaker than we thought. The clear band is being re-checked with Reader v2 + d9v4C and a row score.

findings.title: Our old band was a below-average part of the scan
findings.text: Scan-Quality-Map: 0.37–0.40 for z 9,000–10,000 against a scroll median of 0.41 and 0.54 for the clearest band, where our fit is also our best (0.519 on-sheet).

findings.title: Cracks and recurring zones can look like a signal
findings.text: The strongest PHerc0191 scores (w073 and w074 at depth +2) came from soft blobs along a CT crack band, present at several depths and faintly on the blind side. The strongest PHerc0813 score (w088 with Reader v2 + d9v4C) comes from a bright zone that sits at about the same place on the neighbouring turns w086–w090, as w073–w079 do on PHerc0191; writing does not repeat turn after turn. Neither is writing.

findings.title: Next scroll: PHerc0813
findings.text: Top three at 9.362 µm on two clarity measures, round cross-section, the longest clear stretch, every input published, same orientation as PHerc0191. Then PHerc0358, then PHerc0175A.

findings.title: PHerc0813's geometry passes the Gate B bar
findings.text: Band z 12,000–13,000 with the same recipe as PHerc0191: 0.557 of track points on the sheet and 0.182 of tracks satisfied (0191's clear band: 0.519 / 0.138), the best fit numbers of the campaign. In the CT, w085–w112 (10.5–14.8 cm) show weave over most of their length: more clean papyrus per winding than 0191's best picks, which share a crushed zone. The first eight picks, inked at depths 0 and +1 with three models and with Reader v2 + d9v4C, show no writing; w088's strong score comes from a zone that recurs on the neighbouring turns.

findings.title: Our reading side is the written face
findings.text: On the PHerc. 0343 control, PHerc0191 w073 and PHerc0813 w088 the render's +layer direction points outward and the mesh lies on the inner face of the sheet, the face that carries the 0343 letters. Our reading/blind assignment matches the control; the nulls are not a swapped-side artefact.

findings.title: The method sees ink at 9.36 µm, but the v0.1 flag rule misses text on an unseen scroll
findings.text: AWS run 7, on two known-text segments scanned at the resolution we search. Our render + ink reproduces the published AUCs (PHerc0139 w047: dense_native 0.859, Reader v2 0.860; PHerc0841: Reader v2 + d9v4C 0.83). On PHerc0139 the stroke score sees the text as it saw the PHerc. 0343 letters (reading − blind +0.019 to +0.024, best 4 cm² window 0.054–0.067 against 0.016–0.019 on the blind side). On PHerc0841, a scroll none of the models trained on, the letters show by eye as rows of letter-shaped strokes, yet reading − blind is only +0.001 to +0.009 and the window 1.0–1.4× the blind side: the v0.1 rule would not have singled it out. So windings that stayed under the line could hold text. Known text here shows as rows of elongated strokes; a row score (2.7–4.2 on known text, at most 1.47 on our windings so far) and Reader v2 + d9v4C are now part of the search.

findings.title: Upstream removed the inputs the winner used (Spiral simplification, 2026-09-23)
findings.text: surf-SDT support and the 'phase' dense-spacing mode were deleted from spiral-fitting three weeks before they won a prize. We run the pre-removal commit in a worktree to reproduce the route.

findings.title: #9 Resident-pool sidecars reused after the source store is rebuilt
findings.text: The fitter silently trained on a stale SDT pool (1 of 1,456 bricks) after the store was rebuilt at the same path. Still the case on main; waiting for villa #1883, which changes the same code, before sending a fix.

findings.title: #10 Raw spiral windings render 16–22 % too small (in review, villa #2056)
findings.text: Meshes declare a 20-voxel grid, but on our current PHerc0813 and PHerc0191 fits the nodes are 23–26 voxels apart (26–30 on an earlier fit), so unflattened renders come out 16–22 % small and the recorded areas 34–43 % low; flattened meshes are right. Fix in review as villa #2056: write the measured spacing as the scale and the area in 3D.

findings.title: stroke-score 0.1: triage for ink searches (MIT)
findings.text: Ranks windings, depths and 4 cm² windows by stroke-shaped ink on the reading side against the blind side, with review crops. Calibrated on the PHerc. 343 control and 109 null windings. stroke-score 0.2 (in progress) adds a row score calibrated at search-band height, a stroke-shape score, a neighbour-recurrence check and a known-text control kit.

findings.title: Calibrate on known text cut to your band height
findings.text: Our search bands are about 1 cm tall, so a winding shows at most two lines of text. Known text scored over a whole segment looks far stronger than it would in a band like ours; cut into 1 cm strips, it lands much closer to our null windings. stroke-score's control kit now scores known text at any band height (--band-mm).

findings.title: Ink can be found at 9 µm without a mesh
findings.text: On PHerc0841, a scroll the models never trained on, patches cut along the published surface prediction and inked with the standard 9 µm models find the human-labelled text at AUC 0.76, about 80 % of our full mesh pipeline on the same pixels. A method result on known text, not a discovery; whether it can steer a search is the next test.

findings.title: Test the search rule on the one real win
findings.text: Calibrated on clear known text, our row rule would have missed the PHerc. 0343 First Letters letters (faint, sparse, weak rows). A second line, reading-blind contrast, catches them with no new false alarms on 771 null winding-depths.

next: A model trained on 8.64 µm ink: fine-tune on PHerc. 343's letters (credited) and PHerc1447's published text, test it on letters it never saw, then run it on PHerc0175A and the other 8.64 µm scrolls.
A damage map: score cracks, holes, folds and sheet edges per tile, search the clean papyrus first and discount flags inside damage.
Ink first with a point on every sheet: the PHerc. 343 test is running; if the letters stand out, sweep PHerc0175A again.
The six-model agreement rule on 9.36 µm papyrus (running), then in triage.
Geometry: measure where the fits stack two windings on one sheet, and how much of each band is really covered.

pipeline.title: How the pipeline works
pipeline.lede: From an X-ray scan of a rolled-up scroll to a decision about where to look next, in nine steps. Concepts only; each run page has the details.

stages.title: CT scan
stages.text: An X-ray volume of the rolled scroll. Every slice is a cross-section through all of its wound layers.
stages.alt: CT cross-section through PHerc. 0191: crushed and folded layers of papyrus

stages.title: Find the sheet
stages.text: Fit a spiral model of how the papyrus is wound to sheet tracks traced by the community and to predicted surfaces.
stages.alt: Diagram: a squashed spiral following the wound layers, with track points along it

stages.title: Snap
stages.text: Pull the fitted surface onto the papyrus surface a neural network predicted, so it sits on one real sheet.
stages.by: Erwin Nieuwlaar's snap, m7 surface prediction
stages.alt: Diagram: a dashed fitted line pulled down onto the solid predicted surface

stages.title: Flatten
stages.text: Unroll one winding into a flat sheet, so the papyrus, and any writing on it, appear at true size.
stages.alt: A flattened winding: the crossed fibres of the papyrus are visible

stages.title: Render
stages.text: Sample a thin stack of layers just inside and just outside the surface, like slicing the sheet into leaves.
stages.alt: Diagram: thin layers above and below the sheet surface

stages.title: Detect ink
stages.text: Several public ink models each mark where ink might be. Their maps are combined into one ensemble, for the writing side and for the back.
stages.by: ink_9um, dense_native, Hecate, Reader v2, d9v4C; ensemble after Erwin Nieuwlaar
stages.alt: Ensemble ink map of one flattened winding: mottled, no writing

stages.title: Rank
stages.text: The stroke score points to places where stroke-shaped marks show on the writing side but not on the back; a row score asks whether they line up in rows, as lines of text do.
stages.alt: Review crop: writing side, back and CT side by side

stages.title: Look
stages.text: We check flags and the top-ranked windings by eye against the CT and the back of the sheet, looking for rows of letter strokes. Cracks, voids, folds and zones that recur on neighbouring turns cause most false alarms.
stages.alt: Diagram: three panels labelled writing side, back and CT

stages.title: Gate
stages.text: Decide: go deeper here, move to the next band, or move to the next scroll. A new band or scroll starts again at step 2.
stages.alt: Diagram: a decision with three ways out: go deeper, next band, next scroll

control.title: Positive control
control.text: Known letters go through the same render, ink, rank and look steps: PHerc. 0343 (Erwin Nieuwlaar's First Letters segment, 8.64 µm), and PHerc0139 and PHerc0841 at 9.36 µm, the resolution we search. The letter rows have to light up there; if they did not, a blank result on our scroll would mean nothing. They do, as rows of strokes.
control.alt: Ensemble ink map of the PHerc. 0343 control: two rows of bright letter strokes

items.label: Home GPU box
items.text: The default for everything: it costs nothing extra and the data lives there.

items.label: Cloud GPUs
items.text: Short bursts next to the data, only when it is cost-effective, for example to get a fast answer on something promising.
